Thus, at any rate, they used to call certain periods Olympic and Pythian. The more recent physicians, however, first introduced, in addition to periods, the designation of 'type'. Then some of them held that the same thing is signified by the word 'period' as by 'order' and 'type', while others held that it is not the same. And they attempt to define all these, some in one way and others in another, not only establishing their own definitions but also contradicting those of the others. Now those who have advanced only as far as contentious zeal about definitions, while conceding that one single thing is signified by the three names, 'type', 'period' and 'order', talk less nonsense. But those who call 'period' the time at the interval of which the same thing occurs, and 'type' not simply every such time but only when it is bounded by whole days and nights, these men put forth long and useless nonsense; and having on this account wasted both their own time and that of their pupils, when they come to the sick they are worse than any layman.

For a layman of sense, when he sees someone suffering a paroxysm each day, whether the paroxysm is slightly delayed or comes early, forms some impression of the period called quotidian; and if he should also be diligent and fond of medicine, some notion enters his mind of two tertians or three quartans, and he thinks it right that this be determined by the physicians. It was at this time that I first heard, and marvelled at, those who propose problems in roughly this way: if someone, after a paroxysm lasting five hours, has a remission for two, so that the whole period is of seven hours, and this happens in unbroken succession, what must one take the type to be? I answered him at once that this cannot even happen. For paroxysms of such short duration make their declines long, and for the most part they indeed even reach freedom from fever. 'You,' I said, 'describe a paroxysm of a disease that is most mild, but by the continuity of its periods you then show the same disease to be most deadly.' Since, then, nothing is so useful, and especially in fevers, as to foreknow the beginnings of the paroxysms that are to come, if someone is able right from the beginning to accomplish this by a technical conjecture, he will benefit the patient very greatly throughout the whole disease; but if he is unable to do so right from the beginning, yet becomes able as time goes on, he will help the patient during the remaining time. For the sooner he arrives at foresight of the form of the disease, the longer the time for which he will benefit the sick person. One must therefore try, right from the beginning, to diagnose what sort of fever it is, as has been shown in the commentaries On Crises; and for the most part it is possible to know this securely through the distinguishing signs given in those works. But if someone has not recognised the form of the disease even on this day, but is still at a loss, this man is ignorant of a large part of the art.

All, then, who have written the books on types seem to have given no thought to the benefit to be had from them for prognosis and regimen, but, just as they themselves say, so also to have acted: to have written these things as exercises for the young, closely resembling the riddles posed at dinner.
